brief: Bloomberg macro strategist Simon White argues the Fed under chair Kevin Warsh has tightened financial conditions through inaction rather than active guidance, pushing rate expectations within touching distance of neutral. The terminal rate (the highest implied SOFR yield) sits above the FOMC's longer-run rate projection but still below the Laubach-Williams neutral estimate, so conditions have stayed loose by this measure since around May last year. Today's FOMC decision determines the path: trading risk-reward favors a hold, but a hold would unwind the tightening already achieved, likely raising long-term yields and eventually hitting stocks, signaling that the president is really in charge and delivering a bonanza for inflation with a sharp rise in long-term nominal yields and worsening real stock returns. A hike, assuming it is not read as dovish, would confirm the market's read on Warsh, support the view that the administration prioritizes the 10-year yield over the fed funds rate, and should make conditions tight again, good news for the inflation fight.
